<reason>An exceptionally even, well-grounded debate with no fake sourcing and clean format compliance on both sides. B won the center of the motion by repeatedly converting A's own exhibits into support for the proposition: the Apple ATT flip ("you cannot tell me users consent and that they'll refuse the moment we actually ask"), the equity reversal (the poor pay in the only currency they have), the small-publisher answer (A's own admission that independents can't match giants' targeting), and the closing loyalty-program judo (A's best evidence of "real consent" is explicit, salient opt-in — exactly what the motion demands — while the dossier economy refuses to ask). A landed real, partly unanswered hits: the motion cannot guarantee free services persist (decoupling is "a hope, not a mechanism"), and proactive audits answered B's invisible-harm point. But A's consent examples all involved explicit bargains, never defending the legitimacy of buried cross-site harvesting, leaving B's burden-shift frame as the cleaner decision rule. B's closing misdescribed A as admitting consent never occurs, which keeps the margin moderate.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's ATT flip in Rebuttal 1, completed by the closing loyalty-program turn: A's own proof that genuine consent exists (loyalty cards, personalization opt-ins) became proof that explicit opt-in is feasible and that the industry's twenty-year refusal to ask is a confession — defusing A's "ban in disguise" attack with A's own evidence.</best_rebuttal>
